title: Default values and definite assignment (locals vs fields)
hook: Class fields start at zero or null automatically. Local variables do not — the compiler refuses to let you read a local until every code path assigns it a value.

blocks.text: Every type in C# has a **default value**: `0` for numeric types, `false` for `bool`, `null` for reference types, and all-zero fields for structs. **Fields** on a class or struct, plus array elements and `new T()` for a class, get these defaults automatically. **Local variables** inside a method follow a stricter rule called **definite assignment** — you must assign them on every possible code path before you read them. `int n; Console.WriteLine(n);` is a compile error, not a silent `undefined` like JavaScript.

entries.plainDefinition: The value a type gets when no other value is provided. Numeric types default to 0, `bool` to false, references to null.
A compiler rule that every local variable must be assigned on all paths before its first read.
entries.example: `int retry; Console.WriteLine(retry);` fails with error CS0165.

entries.plainDefinition: An expression that produces the default value of a type. `default` alone infers from context; `default(int)` names the type explicitly.
entries.example: `int retryOk = default;` is the same as `int retryOk = 0;`

blocks.text: Definite assignment prevents a whole class of bugs JavaScript hides. In JavaScript, reading an unassigned `let` gives `undefined`, which silently flows into calculations. In C#, the build stops you. In a CSV importer, a missing column should be an explicit `default`, a nullable `int?`, or a parsed value — never an unassigned local you hope is zero. Fields behave differently: a class field `int _retry` is `0` before your constructor runs.

blocks.title: Fields vs locals
blocks.body: Fields and array slots: automatically zeroed. Locals: you must assign before read. `out` parameters: the callee must assign before returning. Struct locals: every field must be assigned (or use `= default`).

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare a local
items.body: `int retry;` — no value yet. The compiler marks it as "maybe unassigned."

items.title: Compiler tracks every path
items.body: If any path reaches `Console.WriteLine(retry)` without an assignment, the build fails with CS0165.

items.title: Assign on all paths
items.body: An `if/else` that assigns in the `if` but not the `else` still fails. Every branch must assign.

items.title: Use default explicitly
items.body: `int retryOk = default;` assigns 0 immediately. `string? key = default;` assigns null. Prefer explicit `false` or `0` when the meaning matters.

snippet.label: Unassigned local vs explicit default
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: reading `retry` before assignment is a compile error. Line 4: `default` for `int` is `0`. Line 5: `default` for a reference type is `null`. Line 7: writing `false` directly is often clearer than `default` for `bool`.

snippet.label: All branches must assign
snippet.explanation: The compiler analyzes every branch. Line 7 assigns in the `else`; without it, the `else` path would leave `attempts` unassigned and the read on line 10 would fail.

snippet.label: Fields default; struct locals need care
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–3: instance fields are zeroed when the object is created. Lines 8–10: struct locals allow partial field assignment, but you cannot read the struct as a whole until it is definitely assigned (all fields or `= default`).

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Reading a field and assuming a local works the same way — locals are stricter. Using `default` for `string` in a nullable-reference-type project and ignoring the warning (covered in module 07). Declaring a local, filling it only inside an `if` without an `else`, and expecting the compiler to accept the read afterward.

interviewTakeaways: Definite assignment is a compile-time rule for locals (and `out` parameters).
`default` for a reference type is `null`; for `int` it is `0`.
Struct locals must be fully assigned before use unless you write `= default`.
commonPitfalls: Reading a field and assuming a local works the same.
Using `default` for `string` in an NRT context and ignoring the warning (module 07).
Partial assignment of a struct local (`p.X = 1` without `p.Y`) still failing definite assignment.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript locals are `undefined` until set. C# refuses to compile code that reads an unassigned local. TypeScript `strictPropertyInitialization` is the closest analog for class fields.
